## My request:
Take a look at some screens from Contra 3: The Alien Wars for SNES.

In the first 20 seconds of the game, the player is inundated by numerous enemies that come in from the left side of the screen, the right, weapon powerups flying above, robot things coming up from the ground, enemies pitchingn projectiles. It's very busy/noisy. 

I want our game to be like that. Maybe we need to adjust the HP of the monsters and the power of the weapons so it never takes more than 1-3 hits to kill them and have Sean's weapons be a bit faster (not 1 shot per 2-3 sec). Or maybe we shouldn't have Sean be a slower-firing player but instead have Sean and Tony each have their default unique weapon and then have other weapons only be equippable by Tony or Sean (not both)? I'm not sure. Please consult with the Game Mechanics agent and have them do some research and thinking about it.

Also notice how there are more complex platforms in the level (in one of the screenshots). There is a bad guy shooting at the player from atop one. We should have stationary monsters, flying monsters, moving monsters and monsters that pop out from under the ground, from the ceiling, from the background into the foreground and from the viewer's screen area into the normal foreground (as if the monster is jumping in from the viewer's screen into the game). We only have a couple of monsters sketched out right now but we will have more soon. 

Either way, the first level needs a lot of work. It also doesn't have the Clogfather at all in it, which it should at the end.

Let's come up with a plan and some mockups of the new platforming, ideas for how many additional monsters to have, adjustments to weapon power and monster HP so we can have the game be busier and more action-packed. Have engineering present the report.

You are the Level Design agent. Your job will be to help design each level of the game including, but not limited to:



- Assigning platform positions
- Communicating with the Art agent to get create backgrounds and foreground debris that the heroes can jump onto so they're not always jumping onto floating flat platforms (which would be very boring)
- Determining which monsters are present, how many, where they are positioned, etc
- How long each level is horizontally and chronologically
- Possibly creating whole new types of level that are not strictly 2D side-scrolling (for example: Contra 3: The Alien Wars had some levels that were overhead. Maybe we can design a few levels that are not 2D as well (they don't have to be overhead like Contra 3's))
- Anything else related to the creation of levels



Your first task is to talk to the Storyboard agent and Engineering in order to convert the first level of the game, which used to be a tutorial, into a full-length playable level with numerous monsters, platforms, foreground objects to jump on/over, etc.



Feel free to do some research into other 2D Contra (and clone) games if you are not already a level design expert. Don't copy anything directly but feel free to learn from other game designs.

This handoff covers everything recoverable from my current conversation context, including the earlier compacted summary. It is historical evidence, not a fresh inspection of the relocated repository. Your current file inspection and Engineering’s latest delivery records should establish what is actually shipped.

## Role, collaborators, and ownership

Sean assigned this chat Level Design: platform placement, level length and pacing, enemy placement/counts, environmental objects players can climb, coordination with Storyboarding and Art, and eventually alternative level formats.

The immediate objective was to turn the former tutorial into a full first level with dense action, meaningful platforming, varied enemy entrances, and the Clogfather at the end. Sean explicitly requested coordination with Game Mechanics and asked Engineering to present the combined report.

Existing collaborators:

| Role | Chat ID |
|---|---|
| Engineering | `01a1375f-7657-7580-b16e-57a6f5925efd` |
| Game Mechanics | `01a138a7-cc43-7420-a950-55b935ddde25` |
| Bestiary / Art | `01a1388b-2b60-7011-832a-5c6a044e0028` |
| Storyboarding | `01a1387e-545b-7671-943e-3d36a1c88db7` |

Engineering owned integration, base game changes, builds, versions, roadmap, storybook, and the final user report. My edits were assigned subsets, coordinated to avoid shared-file collisions. Mechanics owned weapon balance and later the Widow behavior. Art owned artwork and asset manifests.

The project was relocated to `/Users/sfoley/repos/drain_damage`. Do not recreate `/Users/sfoley/repos/plumbing_inc`.

## User intent and corrections

The original Contra screenshots illustrated the intended feel:

- Many enemies arriving from both horizontal sides.
- Flying threats and powerups.
- Stationary elevated shooters and projectile throwers.
- Ground, ceiling, background-to-foreground, and viewer-to-play-plane entrances.
- Architecture and debris supporting platforms, rather than repeated floating slabs.
- Ordinary enemies generally dying in one to three hits.
- Sean’s weapon firing much faster than the perceived two-to-three-second interval.
- Distinct weapon identities for Tony and Sean, with potentially character-exclusive additional weapons.
- A full level culminating in the Clogfather.

Those were direction and requests for design consultation, not approval of every possible new enemy or entrance mechanic.

Subsequent explicit corrections, relayed through Mechanics/Engineering and implemented within my assigned scope:

1. **Remove every first-level kill-count progress gate.** Replace gated encounters with larger crowds and finite waves along a freely traversable route.
2. **Make the flying spider twice its linear size and durable.** This became a deliberate exception to ordinary enemies’ one-to-three-hit target.
3. **Give the Widow an actual proximity swoop attack matching its magazine description.** A passive fixed hover was superseded.
4. **Audit contrast across every first-level platform.** The initial pale/ivory treatment did not cover the large machinery. The later direction was dank moss/gray-green frames and readable treads, dark undercuts, no beige or glow.
5. **Exactly one checkpoint near halfway through the level.** This superseded three checkpoint machines. One sleeping clone should occupy the sole machine; after dispensing, it should be empty.
6. Preserve three lives, scenery, and free traversal.
7. During the daughter’s playtest, do not foreground or launch the game. All my checks remained headless.

## Last delivered level structure

The active first-level implementation was:

`integrated_first_call.gd` → `opening_trial_game.gd` → `game.gd`

Engineering switched normal Start to the integrated class. The old trial class remained as an internal implementation/test dependency; it was no longer intended as the normal separate timed experience.

The integrated level:

- World width: **9,600 pixels**.
- Temporary completion threshold: **x = 9,450**.
- Player starting x: **85**.
- Opening replacement ends at **x = 3,120**.
- The opening uses the first three platform modules from an earlier 6,000-pixel trial layout.
- Remaining authored scenery stays in its original world coordinates.
- The opening continues beyond 20 seconds; no timed-results stop.
- Checkpoint/respawn does not recreate opening enemies or reset world progress.
- The final delivered checkpoint constant was **`CHECKPOINTS := [4650.0]`**.

### Why x4650

The midpoint between spawn85 and exit9450 is4767.5. The existing cabinet rendering would overlap the next platform beginning at4850 if placed at that exact midpoint.

At checkpoint4650:

- Progress is approximately49% of the playable route.
- The floor is clear between the previous obstacle ending4000 and the next beginning4850.
- Cabinet visible bounds were approximately4643.5–4776.4.
- This leaves approximately73.6 pixels before the next platform.

The existing integrated loops derive machine placement, activation triggers, and enemy-spawn exclusions from `Level.CHECKPOINTS`; changing the constant removed the other placements automatically.

## Ungated encounter implementation

I delivered this in `scripts/integrated_first_call.gd` and updated `tests/integrated_opening.gd`.

### Opening

Twelve finite opening event positions:

`100, 250, 450, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1650, 1900, 2200, 2450`

Their eligibility times were set to zero in the integrated copy of the layout. Position determines when they become eligible; safety and population checks can defer them.

Passing the opening marks remaining unissued opening events unavailable. It does not award kills. Existing live actors persist until normal retirement/death.

### Later waves

| Range | Maximum arrivals |
|---|---:|
| x3500–4800 | 8 |
| x4900–6480 | 10 |
| x6860–8160 | 10 |
| x8400–9380 | 8 |

Total: **36 later runners**, up from the old22 encounter quota, plus the opening’s12 potential events.

Important distinctions:

- These are finite available arrivals, not a guarantee the player must fight all48 enemies.
- Moving past a wave’s range bypasses its unissued remainder.
- No kill requirement blocks forward travel or the temporary exit.
- Arrivals are staggered by at least0.65 seconds.
- At most one arrival is created per encounter update.
- Deferred arrivals do not accumulate into a burst.
- Front/rear entrance selection prefers rear every third arrival and tries the alternate side if needed.
- Entrances are offscreen.
- Player clearance is measured from the expanded visible Flushfiend bounds, not merely its anchor.
- Required clearance:220 pixels.
- Spawn placement avoids scenery, other bodies, opening actors, and checkpoint proximity.
- Checkpoint exclusion: within200 pixels of its location.
- Enemies sufficiently far behind the camera retire without kill credit.
- Retirement threshold used `enemy.pos.x + 38 < camera_x - 320`.
- No live threats are deleted merely to satisfy a population cap.

### Population budget

- Eight bodies normally.
- Six while a live or warning/entering Widow exists.
- One Widow at a time.
- A new Widow is deferred when population is already six.
- Population conservatively counts campaign enemies, live opening actors, and live swarm actors.

Mechanics also wanted two shooters, six hostile bullets, and three independent attack patterns. Opening state already managed those attack budgets. The later waves I added were runners, not additional shooters.

The integrated movement and projectile-solid methods use the replacement level geometry, not the legacy gate geometry.

## Other implementation details worth preserving

### Shared projectile update

The integrated class had to avoid advancing friendly bullets twice through parent/base combat:

2. Restore shots.
3. Run one integrated closest-hit sweep across scenery, opening actors, campaign enemies, and swarm.
4. Temporarily hide friendly shots again when calling the parent’s hostile-shot update.

Do not casually replace this with both parent updates; it previously required explicit single-travel regression coverage.
